Also let, µ = (µ1 , µ2 , . . . , µn ) and µ∗ = (µ∗1 , µ∗2 , . . . , µ∗n ). Then µ [≽m] µ∗ ⇒ Xn:n ≥st Yn:n .

quote: Now the question arises: whether the result of the above theorem can be upgraded to reversed hazard rate ordering or not. Next counter-example shows that this is not possible. Counterexample 3.1 Let, for n = 3 and for r = 1, 2, . . ., h̃n:n (r) and h̃∗n:n (r) denote the reversed hazard rate functions of Xn:n and Yn:n respectively. Now, if µ = (8, 0.8, 0.1) and µ∗ = (7, 1, 0.9) are taken, then although µ [≽m] µ∗ , it can be observed that for r = 5, h̃n:n (r) − h̃∗n:n (r) = 0.0520158 and for r = 2, h̃n:n (r) − h̃∗n:n (r) = −0.0232122, proving that there exist no reversed hazard rate ordering between Xn:n and Yn:n .

quote: Let, X1 , X2 , . . . , Xn and X1∗ , X2∗ , . . . , Xn∗ be two sets of random variables following geometric distribution having parameters q1 , q2 , . . . , qn and q1∗ , q2∗ , . . . , qn∗ respectively. Also let, q = (q1 , q2 , . . . , qn ) and q ∗ = (q1∗ , q2∗ , . . . , qn∗ ). The following theorem shows that, under certain condition X1:n is greater than Y1:n in hazard rate ordering. The proof is straight forward and hence omitted. Theorem 3.3 For i = 1, 2, . . . , n, let Xi and Yi be two sets of mutually independent random variables each satisfying geometric distribution with parameters qi and qi∗ respectively. Then ∏_{i=1}^{n} qi ≥ ∏_{i=1}^{n} qi∗ implies X1:n ≥hr Y1:n .
